title: Postnatal Care (PNC) Schedule & Maternal Recovery
sourceOrganization: Ethiopian Federal Ministry of Health (FMoH) & WHO
summary: Essential post-delivery checkups at 24 hours, day 3, days 7-14, and 6 weeks to ensure maternal healing, baby wellness, and prevent postpartum complications.
keyPoints: Contact 1: Within the first 24 hours after birth before facility discharge.
Contact 2: Day 3 (48 to 72 hours) post-delivery at home or clinic.
Contact 3: Between days 7 and 14 for infant growth and maternal lochia assessment.
Contact 4: At 6 weeks (postpartum family planning initiation, baby immunization, physical recovery exam).
detailedContent: The first 6 weeks postpartum represent the highest risk timeframe for maternal postpartum hemorrhage, puerperal sepsis, and neonatal mortality.
In Ethiopia, Health Extension Workers make scheduled home visits to inspect the umbilical cord stump, check maternal bleeding, and support breastfeeding initiation.
whenToSeeClinician: Seek immediate medical care if you experience foul-smelling vaginal discharge, heavy bleeding soaking a pad an hour, high fever, or severe calf pain.
ethiopiaContext: Delivered through Kebele Health Extension Worker home visits and Health Center maternity outpatient clinics.

title: Exclusive Breastfeeding for 6 Months & Latch Techniques
summary: Exclusive breastfeeding for the first 6 months of life without water or supplementary food provides optimal nutrition and maternal antibodies.
keyPoints: Initiate breastfeeding within the first 1 hour after birth; colostrum (yellowish early milk) is the newborn's first vaccine.
Feed on demand day and night (at least 8 to 12 times in 24 hours).
Do NOT give water, tea, butter, or formula during the first 6 months.
Proper latching: baby's mouth open wide, covering more of the lower areola, chin touching the breast without nipple pain.
detailedContent: In Ethiopian cultural traditions, giving prelacteal feeds (butter or water) was once practiced; health workers have successfully established that pure breast milk contains over 80% water and all vital nutrients.
Breastfeeding also stimulates oxytocin release, contracting the uterus and curtailing postpartum bleeding.
whenToSeeClinician: Contact your midwife or health extension worker if your nipples are cracked, bleeding, or if you develop a painful, hot, reddened breast (possible mastitis).
ethiopiaContext: Promoted nationwide by 40,000+ Health Extension Workers across all rural and urban Ethiopian kebeles.

title: Postpartum Blues, Depression & Maternal Emotional Health
sourceOrganization: World Health Organization (WHO) & Ethiopian Ministry of Health
summary: Differentiates normal transient postpartum blues from postpartum depression (PPD), emphasizing empathetic family support and clinical counseling.
keyPoints: Baby blues: mild crying, fatigue, and mood swings lasting up to 2 weeks post-birth; resolves with family rest and support.
Postpartum depression: persistent sadness, lack of interest in the baby, overwhelming guilt, insomnia, or anxiety lasting >2 weeks.
Affects approximately 1 in 7 mothers globally and is a medical condition, NOT a moral or spiritual failing.
Counseling, support groups, and healthcare provider care are confidential and highly effective.
detailedContent: Dramatic shifts in estrogen and progesterone combined with sleep deprivation make maternal emotional vulnerability common.
In Ethiopian family structures, the traditional 'Aras Bet' (40-day postpartum resting sanctuary) offers vital communal nurturing.
If emotional distress persists, health center clinicians provide compassionate, stigma-free counseling.
whenToSeeClinician: Seek healthcare support if feelings of despair persist longer than 2 weeks, or call 8335 (FMoH) or 6226 (AWSAD) for guidance.
ethiopiaContext: Culturally respected alongside the Ethiopian 'Aras Bet' tradition of maternal recovery and community care.

title: Kangaroo Mother Care (KMC) for Low Birth Weight Newborns
summary: Draft protocol for continuous skin-to-skin contact and frequent breastfeeding for preterm or low birth weight infants (<2.5 kg).
keyPoints: Continuous skin-to-skin contact between mother and baby keeps the newborn warm naturally without electricity-dependent incubators.
Promotes deep infant sleep, stabilizes heart rate and breathing, and improves weight gain.
Both mother and father can participate in continuous skin-to-skin wrapping.
Requires daily weight checks until baby reaches healthy developmental milestones.
detailedContent: Draft clinical guidance: Guidelines for community-initiated KMC by Health Extension Workers for infants born at home in rural woredas.
Awaiting final signoff from the Ethiopian Pediatric Society and neonatal technical working group.
whenToSeeClinician: Any infant born before 37 weeks or weighing under 2.5 kg should be evaluated at a hospital newborn corner.
ethiopiaContext: Established in tertiary and general hospital neonatal wards across all Ethiopian administrative regions.
